Initial Research & Brainstorming Notes

Research 


	•	Themes : Spanish as a mix of ancestor languages. Concept of mixed liquids (one can prevail, but there will always be parts of the other liquid, nothing is "pure").
	•	Spanish (and any language that has had contact with other languages and cultures) can be compared to a liquid. When you wash dishes, a cereal bowl that had milk will always have some milk inside. If one left the bowl with a little milk under a running tap, eventually the bowl would overflow, and the liquid inside would become clearer and clearer, the white milk disappearing. However, the water inside will never be pure. Asymptotically, the amount of milk will always decrease, but it will never reach zero. The only way to purify the water would be to turn the bowl over and let all the liquid out, and then refill the bowl with pure tap water.
	•	Just like different liquids, languages cannot interact without leaving something of themselves inside the other. The resulting language is a distinct concoction that has aspects of all its contributors. We are not going to focus on all the influences of languages like ancient Indo-European, Gothic, Latin, and Mozarabic, and the various dialects of the ancient Iberian Peninsula. Although these contribute to the identity of the Spanish language, the most important thing is to understand that this act of mixing is an inevitable and necessary aspect of a language that moves and spreads.

Conquistadors and the dispersion of Spanish to the new world 


	•	Let's say I found a dam with a dry riverbed in front of it. If I placed a few bowls of milk in various parts of the riverbed and then blew up the dam with dynamite, the resulting violent flood would completely consume the milk to the point that anyone looking at the river could not discern any sign of the milk in the water. However, a scientist analyzing several samples of the river molecularly will find traces of milk along with the water.

The Birth of Spanish 


	•	What linguistic characteristics of the language made it grow and belong?

It is always changing, especially in the days and situations when there was no standardization of the language, or general use of written communication and recording. This allowed the Latin of the Romans to marinate in various regions and towns throughout the peninsula, each developing its own flavor and texture. One of those flavors would become the Spanish we know today.


V1 


V2


The Iberian Peninsula has served as a language blender over the course of its history. Upon the arrival of the Romans in the 2nd century BC, Latin replaced the ancient languages from before. The Spanish spoken today is a direct descendant of Latin. (Hualde et al.) When the Visigoths took charge of the land a few centuries later, they did not manage to replace Latin with their own languages. 


"The ruling Visigothic group constituted a small fraction of the total population of the peninsula, and despite their political supremacy, over time they abandoned their handling of both languages and their speech was entirely assimilated to that of their subjects, who were not only numerically superior but, in that Early Middle Ages, enjoyed a culture more prestigious than that of their rulers. During the course of this period, the majority continued to speak Latin, but, undoubtedly, with considerable variation that increased between one locality and the other." (Penny) 


This is a good example showing that political power does not always rule when we talk about the topic of language development. It was the cultural power held by the subjects of the Visigoths that allowed them to maintain their generational use of Latin that would later give birth to Spanish. We also see that language is always something fluid. Never concrete. It is always changing, especially in the days and situations when there was no standardization of the language, or general use of written communication and recording. This allowed the Latin of the Romans to marinate in various regions and towns throughout the peninsula, each developing its own flavor and texture. One of those flavors would become the Spanish we know today. 


Perhaps the Visigoths managed to make their language [endure], but they did do something considered a catalyst to the development and supremacy of Spanish: they established the city of Toledo as the administrative center of power. The Mozarabs later conquered the land but reigned from this center of power. This created the perfect opportunity for the Castilians to distribute themselves throughout almost all the peninsula after taking the city during the reconquest. During that stage the Castilian influence served as a "wedge" that was inserted to the south of the land and towards both sides, making the Castilians distribute their language through the majority of the country. In the 12th century the Castilian king Alfonso X "the Wise" standardized Castilian and made it the official administrative language of his power. After fermenting in Spain for two more centuries, Castilian was ready to be taken abroad. The union of Queen Isabella with Ferdinand of Aragon and their financing of Christopher Columbus's discovery of the New World began a new age of empires and took Castilian Spanish to distant lands.

Bearing the nickname, "the Wise," this man had an affinity for knowledge. During his reign he and his court produced priceless and innumerable written works. These works include a history of Spain, texts regarding astronomy, medicine and philosophy, and a giant compendium of 2,700 essays that constitute the Siete Partidas--a code of law. (Doubleday, xix) One aspect of his exploration of truth was to make the Castilian language standardized. Most of the Wise King's written works were written in Castilian, and these went all over the country, having a great impact on their readers.

(Hualde 291) However, if there was any doubt that Castilian would become the national language of Spain, it was eliminated during the reign of Alfonso X. Up to this point, we have been able to see that the speech of the inhabitants of Hispania was organized from a mixture of ancient languages to Latin, and how Latin evolved in a particular way in the mouths of the Castilians to resemble modern Spanish. With the reign of Alfonso, we have a language ready to be used. After fermenting in Spain for two more centuries, Castilian was ready to be taken abroad. 



Expansion: Now we arrive at the era of expansion when Spanish truly becomes a global language. It is fascinating that, just like English, Spanish has spread far beyond its point of origin in Spain. Starting from Spain, there are already many countries where the majority of the inhabitants speak Spanish as their native language. This must be due to the imperial spirit of the Spanish just like their English brothers. I believe that the imperial culture of the Europeans contributed to both Spanish and English becoming two of the three most spoken languages in the world. When analyzing the dispersion of Mandarin, we see that it has generally stayed at its point of origin and has not spread from there. This is interesting because it has managed to be the most spoken language in the world without having more than one point of origin. It could be a topic for further exploration. But here the most relevant topic is that the Spanish and the English spread their languages through conquering other lands. 


The union of Queen Isabella of Castile with Ferdinand of Aragon and their financing of Christopher Columbus's discovery of the New World began a new age of empires and took Castilian Spanish to distant lands. In a search for gold and glory, and to expand the kingdom of God, the Spanish sailed their ships west to conquer and colonize the lands of the Americas. In his analysis of the Spanish language titled "Modern Spoken Spanish," Ronald P. Lombardi gives us another illustration of the development, strengthening, and expansion of Castilian: 


"Typically, when native speakers of a language communicate in their new environment in a foreign land, their speaking habits alter with the purpose of facilitating linguistic correspondence. This is precisely what occurred in Latin America, where speakers from Andalusia, Aragon, Leon, Castile, and other regions probably made conscious or subconscious efforts to communicate in a less local and more meaningful way. So, frequently without knowing it, they eventually employed a level of communication that was more standardized than it would have been if the settlers had never left their native regions. The language spoken in the New World eventually served as an agent of change for the Indian languages encountered by the Spanish." (Lombardi 213) 


Here we see that upon arriving in foreign lands, Spanish was strengthened. Faced with the challenge of a new environment, the Spanish had to cooperate linguistically in a different way than in their homeland. One could say that the Spanish language came together during this time, gathering its power more densely, before distributing itself throughout the Americas. Spanish is so common today partly because it had to survive global transportation.

This is precisely what occurred in Latin America, where speakers from Andalusia, Aragon, Leon, Castile, and other regions probably made conscious or subconscious efforts to communicate in a less local and more meaningful way. So, frequently without knowing it, they eventually employed a level of communication that was more standardized than it would have been if the settlers had never left their native regions. The language spoken in the New World eventually served as an agent of change for the Indian languages encountered by the Spanish." (Lombardi 213).


Here we see that upon arriving in foreign lands, Spanish was strengthened. Faced with the challenge of a new environment, the Spanish had to cooperate linguistically in a different way than in their homeland. One could say that the Spanish language came together during this time, gathering its power more densely, before distributing itself throughout the Americas. Spanish is so common today partly because it had to survive global transportation.


Now, we have a language that spans both hemispheres. Just as Latin was sown as a seed in Iberian land so many centuries earlier, Spanish is now sown in the countries of the west. Our exploration ends here at this point in history, but the growth of Spanish is only accelerating. The immigration of millions of Latinos to the United States and the emergence of various modern technologies that allow the transport of people, ideas, and languages all over the world has resulted in an explosion of Spanish because of the momentum created by the Romans, Visigoths, Castilians, and the conquerors of the new world. Because of the need of various powerful peoples to communicate, we have the giant tree that today we call Spanish.

### 1. The Initial Spark: Reading and Inspiration

Your inspiration came from a self-generated conceptual idea, which you articulated in your initial brainstorming notes. You read your own thoughts and recognized a powerful analogy. Specifically, you were inspired by the concept of **Spanish as a mix of ancestor languages**, which you compared to **mixed liquids**.

You explored this idea in depth, reading your own mind-map-like notes:
*   **Core Idea:** "Concept of mixed liquids (one can prevail, but there will always be parts of the other liquid, nothing is 'pure')."
*   **Elaboration:** You developed this with vivid imagery: a cereal bowl with leftover milk, milk in water under a tap (never becoming purely water), and a dam breaking to create a flood that consumes milk but leaves molecular traces.
*   **The Line of Reasoning:** This led you to a core thesis: "Just like different liquids, languages cannot interact without leaving something of themselves inside the other." This became the central argument of your paper—that the mixing of languages is an inevitable, asymptotic process that defines a language's identity.

### 2. Using the Metaphor as Momentum

You didn't just use the metaphor as a garnish; you used it as the **intellectual engine** to structure your entire paper. Here’s how that momentum propelled you forward:

*   **Providing a Framework for Historical Events:** The liquid metaphor gave you a consistent lens through which to interpret the complex history of the Iberian Peninsula. Each historical event became a "mixing" event:
    *   **Romans + Natives:** The introduction of Latin, the "base liquid."
    *   **Visigoths:** A small amount of a new "liquid" (Gothic) that ultimately dissolved into the Latin base, leaving traces but not overwhelming it.
    *   **Mozarabs/Moors:** Another wave of liquids added to the blend.
    *   **Reconquista & Castilians:** The Castilian "wedge" acted as a force that distributed and concentrated the existing mixture.
    *   **Colonization of the Americas:** The Spanish liquid was poured into a new container, interacting with indigenous languages to create a new, distinct variety of the mixture.

*   **Driving Draft Iterations (V1-V5):** The metaphor was present from the very beginning. As you moved from draft to draft, you refined how you expressed this core idea.
    *   In early drafts (V2, V3), you laid out the historical facts but framed them within the context of this mixing.
    *   In V4, you began to use more evocative, metaphorical language drawn from the same conceptual family: the peninsula as a "language blender," Latin "marinating" in various regions, Castilian "fermenting" in Spain.
    *   In the final essay, the explicit "milk and water" analogy is gone, but its conceptual DNA is woven throughout. You use words like "blender," "marinate," "flavor and texture," "fermenting," and the final image of a "giant tree." This shows you distilled the original idea into more academic language while retaining the core organic, blending concept. The tree metaphor in the conclusion is a natural extension of the growth and life implied by the liquid/culinary metaphors.

*   **Creating a Cohesive Narrative:** The metaphor helped you connect disparate historical facts into a single, compelling story. Instead of a list of conquests and rulers, you presented a narrative of inevitable fusion. The momentum came from tracing this fusion from its ancient origins to its global expansion.

In summary, you read your own abstract idea—the liquid metaphor—and recognized it as a powerful tool for reasoning. You used it to frame your research, structure your argument chronologically, and transform a collection of historical facts into a cohesive narrative. That initial spark of an analogy provided the thematic momentum that carried you through all five drafts and culminated in a polished, well-reasoned final essay.
